- Shared library modules: `timeline.py`, `llm_clients.py`, `asset_cache.py`, `theme_schema.py`, `text_match.py`, `arrangement_rules.py`, `enriched_arrangement.py`

```text
  core/
  stages/
  reviewers/
tests/
examples/
remotion/
scripts/
```

That would require updating imports/tests and probably adding `pyproject.toml` with console scripts, so it’s a real refactor, not just file moving.

Will we lose any tools?

> AGENT

No, not if we do the cleanup correctly.

The top-level Python files are mostly “tools” only because they’re scripts. We can move them into a package and expose the same commands through wrappers or console scripts, so usage can stay equivalent:

```bash
python pipeline.py ...
python cut.py ...
```

can become either:

```bash
artagents pipeline ...
artagents cut ...
```

or we can keep thin root wrappers like `pipeline.py` that import from the new package.

The only things I’d remove are non-tool junk: `_fixture_case.py` if it’s only test support, stale root `package.json` workspace marker if no longer needed, and ignored local caches like `.DS_Store`, `__pycache__`, `.pytest_cache`, `.tmp`, `.claude`, `.megaplan`.

So: no tool loss required. It’s mostly reorganizing and adding compatibility shims.

intro_label = f\"intro_sponsor{index}\"\n+        lines.append(f\"[{outro_label}][{label}]overlay=x=W-w-110:y=H-h-95[outro_sponsor{index}]\")\n+        outro_label = f\"outro_sponsor{index}\"\n+        next_input += 1\n+    lines.append(f\"[{intro_label}][{body_label}][{outro_label}]concat=n=3:v=1:a=0[vout]\")\n+    return \";\\n\".join(lines) + \"\\n\"\n+\n+\n+def _talk_from_raw(raw: dict[str, Any]) -> Talk:\n+    speaker = str(raw[\"speaker\"])\n+    title = str(raw[\"title\"])\n+    return Talk(\n+        slug=str(raw.get(\"slug\") or _slugify(f\"{speaker} {title}\")),\n+        speaker=speaker,\n+        title=title,\n+        source=str(raw[\"source\"]),\n+        start=float(raw[\"start\"]),\n+        end=float(raw[\"end\"]),\n+    )\n+\n+\n+def _print_context(segments: list[dict[str, Any]], start: float, end: float, radius: float) -> None:\n+    for segment in segments:\n+        seg_start = float(segment.get(\"start\") or 0.0)\n+        seg_end = float(segment.get(\"end\") or seg_start)\n+        if seg_end >= start - radius and seg_start <= end + radius:\n+            print(f\"  {_fmt_time(seg_start)} {str(segment.get('text') or '').strip()}\")\n+\n+\n+def _textfile(tmpdir: Path, name: str, value: str) -> Path:\n+    path = tmpdir / name\n+    path.write_text(value + \"\\n\", encoding=\"utf-8\")\n+    return path\n+\n+\n+def _drawtext_font() -> str:\n+    for path in (\n+        \"/System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental/Arial Bold.ttf\",\n+        \"/System/Library/Fonts/Supplemental/Arial.ttf\",\n+        \"/Library/Fonts/Arial.ttf\",\n+    ):\n+        if Path(path).is_file():\n+            return path\n+    return \"\"\n+\n+\n+def _require_ffmpeg() -> None:\n+    if shutil.which(\"ffmpeg\") is None:\n+        raise SystemExit(\"ffmpeg is required\")\n+\n+\n+def _fold(value: str) -> str:\n+    return value.lower().replace(\"ú\", \"u\").replace(\"á\", \"a\").replace(\"é\", \"e\").replace(\"í\", \"i\").replace(\"ó\", \"o\")\n+\n+\n+def _slugify(value: str) -> str:\n+    value = _fold(value)\n+    value = re.sub(r\"[^a-z0-9]+\", \"-\", value).strip(\"-\")\n+    return re.sub(r\"-{2,}\", \"-\", value)[:96]\n+\n+\n+def _fmt_time(seconds: float) -> str:\n+    seconds = max(0.0, seconds)\n+    whole = int(seconds)\n+    return f\"{whole // 3600:02d}:{(whole % 3600) // 60:02d}:{whole % 60:02d}\"\n+\n+\n+if __name__ == \"__main__\":\n+    raise SystemExit(main())\n*** End Patch\n"
```json
}
```

> DEVELOPER

Sorry, why can't we just use this via the file API or the OpenAI API or something like that rather than trying to do it locally?

> DEVELOPER

Is that not gonna take ages?

> AGENT

Yes, we should use the API if we have a key. I initially went local because this shell has no `OPENAI_API_KEY`/`ANTHROPIC_API_KEY`/`GEMINI_API_KEY` in the environment, and I didn’t want to go spelunking through `.env` files or print secrets.

The caveat is that the OpenAI audio transcription endpoint has a 25 MB upload limit per audio file according to the official speech-to-text docs, so we still need to chunk the recordings first. The Files API can store larger files, but that is not the same as handing a 600 MB or 1.2 GB recording directly to the transcription endpoint. Sources: OpenAI speech-to-text guide and Files API reference.

The faster path is:
1. Extract/compress audio to small chunks, probably 5-10 minute `m4a` chunks under 25 MB.
2. Send chunks to `gpt-4o-transcribe` or `gpt-4o-transcribe-diarize`.
3. Stitch chunk timestamps back to global video time.
4. Use that transcript to find host intros, speaker names, and applause/break boundaries.
5. Render the split videos.

That should be much better than full local transcription. I’m going to stop the local jobs and wire the chunked OpenAI path into the tool. It will only run once a key is available to the process.

```json
{
```
```json
  "patch": "*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: /Users/user_c042661f/Documents/reigh-workspace/ArtAgents/README.md\n@@\n ## Pure-generative and no-audio modes\n \n `pipeline.py` also supports an audio-backed no-video path:\n@@\n No-audio mode runs `pool_merge`, `arrange`, `cut`, and optionally `render`. It skips source-video analysis plus `transcribe`, `refine`, `editor_review`, and `validate`, and the emitted timeline has no `a1` track.\n \n+## Event Talk Splitting\n+\n+For long conference or livestream recordings, do not start with local Whisper unless API keys are unavailable. Use the existing OpenAI-backed `transcribe.py` path, which already does silence-aware chunking, skips mostly silent chunks, keeps files below the transcription upload limit, and stitches chunk timestamps back into source time.\n+\n+Recommended flow:\n+\n+```bash\n+python3 transcribe.py \\\n+  --audio talk-day.wav \\\n+  --out runs/event/transcript \\\n+  --env-file /path/to/.env \\\n+  --model whisper-1 \\\n+  --language en \\\n+  --max-chunk-sec 600\n+\n+python3 event_talks.py ados-sunday-template --out runs/event/talks.json\n+python3 event_talks.py search-transcript --transcript runs/event/transcript/transcript.json\n+python3 event_talks.py render --manifest runs/event/talks.json --out-dir runs/event/rendered\n+```\n+\n+If the source is a large MP4, extract a mono audio file first and pass that to `transcribe.py`; otherwise ffmpeg can spend time scanning video while it only needs audio:\n+\n+```bash\n+ffmpeg -y -i source.mp4 -vn -ac 1 -ar 16000 -c:a pcm_s16le runs/event/source.wav\n+```\n+\n+The talk manifest is the source of truth for final cuts. Fill each talk with `source`, `start`, and `end` after checking the transcript against the public schedule, host intros, applause, break cards, and contact-sheet thumbnails. Rendered talk videos and intermediate transcripts belong under `runs/`, which is ignored by git.\n+\n ## Effects and themes\n \n Shared render effects live at workspace root under `effects/<id>/`. Each effect folder must contain `component.tsx`, `schema.json`, `defaults.json`, and `meta.json`; `preview.mp4` is optional. The catalog is generated by scanning that directory, not by maintaining a hand-written list.\n*** End Patch\n"
}
```

> AGENT

Implemented `visual_understand.py`.

What it does:
- Accepts one image via `--image`.
- Accepts multiple images via repeated `--image`.
- Samples specific video frames via `--video ... --at ...`.
- Builds a numbered contact sheet automatically for multiple frames/images.
- Defaults to `gpt-5.4-mini`, `detail=low`, 4 columns, max 20 frames.
- Supports model comparison with `--compare-model`.
- Saves JSON results with usage and response IDs.

Example:

```bash
python3 visual_understand.py \
  --video "ADOS 2026 - Day 3 (Deep Dives & Talks) (1).mp4" \
  --at 0,20,40,60,80,100,120,140,160 \
  --query "Which numbered frames are holding/title screens or setup screens that should be removed before the talk starts, and which are usable talk frames to keep?" \
  --out runs/ados-talks/analysis/ziv-start-vision-query.json \
  --env-file /path/to/.env
```

Tested on the Ziv start frames. All three models agreed:
- Remove frames `1-5`: lunch / “we’ll be back” holding screen.
- Keep frames `6-9`: speaker/stage/slides are visible.

Model comparison:
- `gpt-5.4-mini`: 2.28s, same answer, cheapest/default choice.
- `gpt-5.4`: 5.76s, same answer, more verbose.
- `gpt-5.2`: 2.87s, same answer.

So for this tool I’d use `gpt-5.4-mini` by default and only switch to a larger model or `--detail high` when text is tiny or the visual decision is subtle.

Files added/updated:
- `artagents/visual_understand.py`
- `visual_understand.py`
- `tests/test_visual_understand.py`
- `README.md`
- `SKILL.md`

Verified with:
- `pytest tests/test_visual_understand.py`
- `python -m py_compile artagents/visual_understand.py visual_understand.py`

I used the OpenAI Responses API image-input path from the official docs: https://platform.openai.com/docs/guides/images-vision

> AGENT

Yes, I understand the workflow now, and the new tool helps, but it should be used as one signal rather than the whole decision-maker.

**What I Tested**

I ran visual review on two contact sheets:

- Start boundaries for all five talks: `runs/ados-talks/analysis/all-start-boundaries-fast.json`
- End boundaries for all five talks: `runs/ados-talks/analysis/all-end-boundaries-fast.json`

Then I reran both with `--mode best`:

- `runs/ados-talks/analysis/all-start-boundaries-best.json`
- `runs/ados-talks/analysis/all-end-boundaries-best.json`

**What Worked**

The tool is easy to query. One command can review 15-20 candidate frames at once, which is much better than manually opening thumbnails.

For obvious cases, fast mode works well:
- It correctly identified lunch/wait frames.
- It correctly picked Ziv’s first good talk frame at `02:20`.
- It correctly separated obvious host/setup frames from active talk frames.

**Where It Struggles**

Fast mode sometimes miscopies timestamps in its answer. The frame numbers are reliable, but the prose timestamp can be wrong. So the tool should return or post-process structured frame-number decisions against our own frame table, not trust copied timestamps from the model.

Best mode is stricter. It tends to remove more intro/title/setup frames and keep only frames where the talk is clearly underway. That is useful for clean visual cuts, but it can cut off spoken greetings or early remarks if used alone.

Example:
- Transcript says Ingi starts speaking at `01:11:36`.
- Best visual mode prefers frame `20` at `01:11:55`, because earlier frames still look like setup/laptop movement.
- So visual-only would cut too late if we care about preserving first spoken words.

**Best Process**

1. Use transcript/audio to find likely semantic boundaries: speaker starts, title spoken, “thank you”, host handoff.
2. Sample frames around those boundaries, usually 3-5 frames per talk.
3. Run `visual_understand.py` in default `fast` mode.
4. If fast is ambiguous, sloppy, or the cut matters, rerun the same contact sheet with `--mode best`.
5. Final boundary should combine:
   - transcript start/end,
   - visual cleanliness,
   - OCR holding-screen detection,
   - silence/applause/host handoff cues.

**Main Bottleneck**

The bottleneck is choosing candidate frames to query in the first place. Once the frames are selected, querying is easy. The missing tool is an `auto-boundary-review` command that automatically gathers frames around transcript/OCR/silence candidate points, runs visual understanding, and outputs suggested manifest edits with confidence.

The visual tool is useful now, but the next improvement should be making it part of a boundary-review pipeline rather than something we manually drive one contact sheet at a time.

> AGENT

Yes, correct. The big improvement is packaging existing asset-level analysis so agents do not manually guess frames.

I found the existing pipeline pieces:

- `scenes.py` -> PySceneDetect scene boundaries into `scenes.json`
- `shots.py` -> representative scene frames into `shots.json`
- `quality_zones.py` -> silence/black ranges into `quality_zones.json`
- `event_talks.py find-holding-screens` -> OCR wait/holding/title cards
- `transcribe.py` -> transcript segments with timestamps
- `hype.metadata.json` already stores these as asset-level refs under `sources[asset_key]`

So yes: this data belongs on the asset/source level, not in the timeline. Timelines should reference assets and edits; source analysis should live beside the asset and be referenced through metadata.

I added `boundary_candidates.py` to package this into a standard review object. It takes manifest boundaries plus transcript/scenes/shots/holding refs and emits candidate frame sets for visual review.

Example:

```bash
python3 boundary_candidates.py \
  --asset-key main \
  --video source.mp4 \
  --manifest runs/event/talks.json \
  --transcript runs/event/transcript/transcript.json \
  --scenes runs/event/scenes.json \
  --shots runs/event/shots/shots.json \
  --holding-screens runs/event/holding-screens.json \
  --out runs/event/boundary-candidates.json
```

The output now includes:

- `asset_key`
- `asset_analysis`
- `metadata_source_refs`
- per-boundary candidate timestamps
- ready-to-run `visual_understand.py` commands

I also updated `visual_understand.py` to nudge agents: if they try to query a video without `--at`, it tells them to run `boundary_candidates.py` first.

The bottleneck is now much clearer: not “can we ask vision,” but “have we generated/reused the asset analysis refs.” Once those exist, frame candidate selection becomes mechanical.

Verified with:

```bash
pytest tests/test_boundary_candidates.py tests/test_visual_understand.py
python -m py_compile artagents/boundary_candidates.py boundary_candidates.py
```

I also generated a real ADOS candidate package at:

`runs/ados-talks/analysis/day3-partial-boundary-candidates.json`

> AGENT

Yes, I tested it on the real ADOS task.

The vision tool worked for the practical problem: it correctly identified the lunch/wait frames and helped confirm that Ziv should start at `02:20`, not during the lunch card or stage setup. It also made the weakness obvious: vision alone can be too aggressive or too late because it judges what looks clean, while transcript/audio tells us when the speaker actually starts. So the right workflow is transcript + holding-screen OCR + candidate frames + vision review, not vision by itself.

I also added the process to `SKILL.md`: agents are now told to generate/reuse asset-level analysis first (`scenes`, `shots`, holding screens, transcript), then package candidates with `boundary_candidates.py`, then query with `visual_understand.py`.

> AGENT

Yes, that’s exactly what the crop-review mode is for.

For best crop from one image/frame, I’d run the vision tool with multiple candidate crops in one numbered contact sheet, then ask it which works best:

```bash
PYENV_VERSION=3.11.11 python visual_understand.py \
  --image path/to/frame.jpg \
  --crop-aspect 9:16 \
  --crop-position left,center,right \
  --query "Which crop works best for a vertical video? Prefer the one that keeps the speaker visible and preserves useful slide context."
```

For “different slices”:

```bash
# 9:16 vertical crops across a wide frame
--crop-aspect 9:16 --crop-position left,center,right

# 16:9 horizontal crops through a tall frame
--crop-aspect 16:9 --crop-position top,center,bottom

# multiple crop shapes at once
--crop-aspect 9:16,1:1 --crop-position left,center,right
```

I tested this on the actual Ziv frame, and the tool picked the center `9:16` crop as the best compromise between speaker and slide context. Current limitation: it supports named crop positions, not arbitrary numeric slice anchors yet. The next useful upgrade would be something like `--crop-anchor 0.25,0.5` or `--crop-window 9:16:x=0.2:y=0.5` so we can test very precise slices beyond left/center/right/top/bottom.

The gap was in the event-talk section of `SKILL.md`: it lists:

```bash
python3 event_talks.py render --manifest runs/event/talks.json --out-dir runs/event/rendered
```

That command currently means the ffmpeg-only event renderer. It doesn’t warn that this bypasses the canonical Remotion/Reigh timeline path, and it doesn’t say “prefer emitting `hype.timeline.json` + `hype.assets.json` and rendering through `render_remotion.py` for branded/motion graphics work.”

> DEVELOPER

Were the instructions not general enough? ("if you're rendering a video..."

> AGENT

They were general enough. I missed the implication.

The skill doc and README together make the intended hierarchy pretty clear:

- General repo rendering: use `cut.py --render --renderer remotion` / `render_remotion.py`.
- Event talk splitting: has a convenience `event_talks.py render` command.
- For anything with real motion graphics, branding, intro/outro, layout, or reusable video composition, the general Remotion renderer should win over the convenience ffmpeg renderer.

The ambiguity is that the event-talk command is named `render`, so it looked like the local workflow for this exact task. But that’s not a good enough reason once the task became “make a polished branded video.” At that point I should have read the rendering docs, seen Remotion was already the default, and routed it through that.

A small skill-doc improvement would prevent this happening again:

```md
For any final or branded video render, prefer the canonical Remotion renderer:
cut.py --render --renderer remotion or render_remotion.py.

event_talks.py render is a quick ffmpeg-only proof renderer for boundary checks
and rough review. Do not use it for polished intros, outros, lower-thirds, sponsor
layouts, or ADOS/Reigh-style motion graphics unless the user explicitly asks for
a fast ffmpeg proof.
```

That should go in the Event Talk Splitting section and maybe the Validation/Rendering section too.

> DEVELOPER

why was it so slow?

> AGENT

Because full Remotion was rendering the entire 11.6-minute talk frame by frame through Chrome.

At 30fps, that’s about `20,925` frames. For every frame, Remotion/Chromium had to load the video, composite the overlays, screenshot/render the frame, and hand it to the compositor. The process was only running at concurrency `2`, and it also writes a lot of temporary frame data while rendering. With only ~`3.5GB` free disk, it eventually failed with:

`ENOSPC: no space left on device`

So the slow path was:

`long source video + every frame through Remotion + low concurrency + little free disk`

The faster fix was to use Remotion only where it helps: animated intro/outro cards. Then ffmpeg handles the long talk video pass, which is much faster for plain video scaling, overlays, audio, and concatenation. That completed in minutes instead of half an hour-plus.

> DEVELOPER

Do you think we should just make the entry animations and exit animations via eMotion and then attach them to the video? Is there a more efficient flow we should have? And if we had more space on our computer, would it have been a lot faster or would that not meaningfully impact it?

> AGENT

Yes. For long event talks, the efficient flow should be:

1. Use Remotion for short designed pieces:
   - intro card
   - outro card
   - maybe animated lower-third as a short transparent overlay if needed

2. Use ffmpeg for the long source-video pass:
   - trim talk
   - scale/pad/crop
   - add static logo
   - add lower-third
   - concat intro + talk + outro

That is exactly what `--renderer remotion-wrapper` now does. It keeps Remotion where it’s valuable and avoids sending 20k+ mostly-normal video frames through Chrome.

More disk space would have prevented the `ENOSPC` failure, but it would not have made the render meaningfully faster. The bottleneck was CPU/GPU/Chromium frame rendering, not just disk. More free space means “it finishes”; higher Remotion concurrency and a faster machine mean “it finishes faster.”

The next better version would be:
- Remotion renders intro/outro once per talk.
- Remotion optionally renders transparent `.mov` overlays for lower-thirds.
- ffmpeg composites those overlays onto the talk.
- Cache intro/outro/overlay assets by talk metadata hash so rerenders only rebuild changed pieces.
- Add a disk-space preflight before full Remotion renders.

> AGENT

Opened Calvin.

Yes, I can see it. The off-screen issue is already in the source recording: Calvin walks/pans near the frame edge and the camera operator sometimes loses him. Our wrapper is not cropping the body video; the filter is just full-frame scale/pad from 1280x720 to 1920x1080.

The jittery pan feeling is mainly because the source is low-bitrate 720p, then we upscaled it to 1080p. That makes the camera pan artifacts and motion judder more obvious. Frame timing itself looks regular at 30fps, so it does not look like dropped-frame jitter from our render.

Best fix: remake Calvin at native 1280x720 instead of upscaling to 1080p. It will not recover parts where he is genuinely out of frame, but it should feel less harsh/jittery and look closer to the source. We could try stabilization or 60fps interpolation, but that may add weird artifacts and won’t solve the camera losing him.

```json
{
```
```json
  "patch": "*** Begin Patch\n*** Update File: /Users/user_c042661f/Documents/banodoco-workspace/brain-of-bndc/src/features/admin_chat/agent.py\n@@\n-- share_to_social(message_id?, message_link?, tweet_text?, media_urls?, action?, target_post?, reply_to_tweet?, text_only?, schedule_for?, platform?) — share or schedule publishing to X/Twitter. Supports post, reply, retweet, and quote actions, including direct posting without a Discord message: provide tweet_text and optionally media_urls (e.g. Supabase video links). For retweets, provide `action=retweet` and `target_post`. For quote tweets, provide `action=quote` and `target_post` (embeds the target tweet below your text/media). `schedule_for` must be ISO-8601 with timezone. `target_post` or `reply_to_tweet` accepts a tweet URL or ID. **Thread replies default to text-only** so a follow-up doesn't reattach the parent tweet's media — pass `text_only=false` explicitly if you DO want a reply to also include the source message's media. Immediate success returns `tweet_url`/`tweet_id` plus `publication_id`; scheduled success returns `publication_id` with queued status. If `already_shared` is true on a rerun, cite the returned existing `tweet_url` instead of treating it as a failure.\n+- share_to_social(message_id?, message_link?, tweet_text?, media_urls?, action?, target_post?, reply_to_tweet?, text_only?, schedule_for?, platform?) — share or schedule publishing to social. Supports X/Twitter post/reply/retweet/quote actions and YouTube post actions via Zapier (`platform=\"youtube\"`). For direct YouTube uploads, provide `media_urls` with a reachable video URL and `tweet_text`; the first non-empty line becomes the title and the full text becomes the description unless Zapier/route metadata overrides it. For retweets, provide `action=retweet` and `target_post`. For quote tweets, provide `action=quote` and `target_post` (embeds the target tweet below your text/media). `schedule_for` must be ISO-8601 with timezone. `target_post` or `reply_to_tweet` accepts a tweet URL or ID. **Thread replies default to text-only** so a follow-up doesn't reattach the parent tweet's media — pass `text_only=false` explicitly if you DO want a reply to also include the source message's media. Immediate success returns `provider_url`/`provider_ref` plus legacy `tweet_url`/`tweet_id` when applicable, and `publication_id`; scheduled success returns `publication_id` with queued status. If `already_shared` is true on a rerun, cite the returned existing `provider_url` instead of treating it as a failure.\n@@\n-- Share to social media with `share_to_social`, including scheduled posts/replies/retweets/quote tweets. Supports direct posting without a Discord message: provide tweet_text and optionally media_urls (e.g. Supabase video links). For retweets, provide action=retweet and target_post. How it works:
```

- Sends Zapier: `title`, `description`, `media_url`, `media_urls`, `privacy_status`, `tags`, `playlist_id`, `made_for_kids`, plus source metadata.
- For direct uploads, pass a reachable video URL in `media_urls`; the first line of `tweet_text` becomes the title, full `tweet_text` becomes the description unless metadata/route config overrides it.

Example tool intent:
```json
{
  "platform": "youtube",
  "media_urls": ["https://.../video.mp4"],
  "tweet_text": "Talk title\nDescription text here"
}
```

> DEVELOPER

Why in brain_of_bndc? Why not a shared repo both use? That feels like terribel structure

> AGENT

You’re right. I put it in `brain-of-bndc` because that’s where the only existing social publishing abstraction lived: `SocialPublishService`, routes, scheduling, admin `share_to_social`, and tests. But structurally, that makes YouTube publishing a Discord-bot feature, which is wrong for ArtAgents video publishing.

Better shape:

- `banodoco-social` should be the shared publishing package/tool.
- It should expose a simple CLI/API like:
  ```bash
  banodoco-social publish youtube --video path-or-url --title ... --description ... --tags ...
  ```
- `brain-of-bndc` should call that shared tool for Discord/admin social posts.
- `ArtAgents` should call the same tool for rendered talk uploads.
- Credentials and Zapier/direct YouTube config should live behind that shared tool, not inside either app.
- Platform providers should live there: `youtube_zapier`, later `youtube_api`, `x`, `instagram`, etc.

So yes, the right follow-up is to move this out of `brain-of-bndc` into `/Users/user_c042661f/Documents/banodoco-workspace/banodoco-social`, then make `brain-of-bndc` depend on/call it. That keeps ArtAgents from importing Discord bot code just to upload videos.

> DEVELOPER

is 'node' the right name?

> AGENT

Probably not for this.

For ArtAgents, “node” seems to mean an executable media/pipeline unit: render, transcribe, visual understand, split talks, etc. Publishing to YouTube is more of an **output destination** or **distribution target**, not a content-processing node.

Better names:

- **Publisher**: best fit for `banodoco-social`.
  - `youtube_publisher`
  - `social_publisher`
  - `publishers/youtube.py`

- **Sink**: good if we think in pipeline terms.
  - A render outputs media, then a sink ships it somewhere.
  - `youtube_sink`, `reigh_sink`, `filesystem_sink`

- **Exporter**: good if it transforms/ships finished artifacts.
  - `youtube_exporter`
  - `reigh_exporter`

- **Destination**: good for config UX.
  - `destination: youtube`
  - `destination: reigh`

I’d use **publisher** for the shared repo/API and maybe **sink** inside ArtAgents if we want pipeline graph language.

So not:
```text
nodes/youtube_publish
```

Better:
```text
artagents/publishers/youtube.py
banodoco_social/publishers/youtube.py
```

Or, if we want it discoverable like nodes:
```text
artagents/outputs/youtube.py
artagents/destinations/youtube.py
```

My recommendation: call this category **publishers**, and keep “nodes” for transformations/analysis/rendering steps.

So the user-facing name should probably stay plain:


or:

I’d avoid making people think in architecture categories unless they’re developing the system.

A better split:

- Internal shared package function: `publish_youtube_video`
- Internal category if needed later: `outputs` or `publishing`

So the docs/tools should say:
> Upload a finished video to YouTube via Banodoco Social.

Not:
> Run the YouTube publisher node.

For the actual ADOS workflow, the agent should see something like:
```bash
python3 pipeline.py upload-youtube \
  --video-url ... \
  --title ... \
  --description ...
```

That’s closer to what it does and easier to understand.

> DEVELOPER

So what's below a conductor?

> AGENT

Below a **conductor**, I’d think in terms of **actions** or **steps**, not “nodes”.

For normal people:

- **Conductor** = runs a workflow.
- **Step** = one thing inside that workflow.
- **Action** = an operation the agent/tool can perform.
- **Tool** = the executable capability behind an action.

So for ADOS:

```text
Conductor: publish ADOS talks
Steps:
  1. render talk videos
  2. upload videos somewhere reachable
  3. upload to YouTube
  4. write metadata/results
```

The third one should probably be called:
```text
Upload to YouTube
```

Not:
```text
YouTube publisher node
```

If we need internal structure:

```text
conductors/
  ados_publish_talks/

actions/
  upload_youtube/
  render_event_talks/
  transcribe_video/
  find_boundaries/
```

I’d reserve **node** only if we are literally building a graph/flow editor or a typed DAG where each block has inputs/outputs. Otherwise **step/action/tool** is much clearer.

> DEVELOPER

In an orchesra, kinda situation, like what's the group of people individually who are conducted or led such an orchestraor

> AGENT

In an orchestra, the people below / led by the **conductor** are usually:

- **Musicians** or **players**: the individual people.
- **Instrumentalists**: if you want a more formal word.
- **Sections**: groups of players, like strings, woodwinds, brass, percussion.
- **Principals**: the lead player within a section.
- **Ensemble**: the whole group being conducted.

For our naming metaphor:

- **Conductor** = coordinates the workflow.
- **Section** = a grouped capability area, like video, audio, publishing.
- **Player** or **Performer** = an individual executable action/tool.
- **Score** = the written plan/recipe/manifest.
- **Performance** = one run of the workflow.

So instead of “node”, maybe:

```text
conductors/
sections/
players/
scores/
```

For “upload to YouTube”, that would be a **player** in the **publishing section**.

But I’d be careful: “player” is metaphorically nice, but less instantly clear than “tool” or “action”. A hybrid could work:

```text
actions/        # user/developer clear
conductors/     # orchestration metaphor
```

If you want to lean into the orchestra metaphor, **players** is the closest answer.

> DEVELOPER

hmm, other idaeas in that direction?

> AGENT

Yeah, a few metaphor families around “conductor” that might fit better than “node”:

**Orchestra Terms**
- **Player**: individual executable capability. Friendly, but maybe a bit vague.
- **Performer**: clearer than player, still human-ish.
- **Section**: group of related performers/tools, like video, audio, publishing.
- **Part**: the written role for one instrument; could map to a step definition.
- **Score**: the full workflow plan/recipe.
- **Movement**: a major phase in a longer workflow.
- **Cue**: trigger/instruction for an action.
- **Arrangement**: configured version of a workflow.

**Theatre / Production**
- **Cast**: available tools/agents.
- **Role**: what a tool does.
- **Scene**: a phase or chunk of work.
- **Cue**: command to perform something.
- **Stagehand**: background utility/tool. Fun but maybe too cute.

**Film / Studio**
- **Crew**: tools/agents that do the work.
- **Department**: grouped capability area.
- **Shot**: maybe already domain-specific here, so avoid overloading.
- **Take**: one run/attempt.
- **Cut**: output version, but already used.

My best picks:

```text
Conductor -> coordinates
Score -> workflow/recipe
Cue -> executable instruction
Performer -> individual tool/action
Section -> grouped performers
```

Example:

```text
scores/ados_talk_upload.json
conductors/ados_publish.py
sections/publishing/
performers/upload_youtube.py
performers/stage_video.py
```

If you want less metaphor and more clarity:

```text
conductors/
workflows/
actions/
```

I’d probably use **performers** if you want the orchestra feel, or **actions** if you want people to instantly understand it.

prog=\"pipeline.py performers\",\n+        description=\"List, inspect, validate, and run ArtAgents performers.\",\n+    )\n+    subparsers = parser.add_subparsers(dest=\"command\", required=True)\n+\n+    list_parser = subparsers.add_parser(\"list\", help=\"List available performers.\")\n+    list_parser.add_argument(\"--json\", action=\"store_true\", help=\"Emit inspect_parser.add_argument(\"performer_id\")\n+    inspect_parser.add_argument(\"--json\", action=\"store_true\", help=\"Emit machine-readable JSON.\")\n+    inspect_parser.set_defaults(handler=_cmd_inspect)\n+\n+    validate_parser = subparsers.add_parser(\"validate\", help=\"Validate performer metadata.\")\n+    validate_parser.add_argument(\"performer_id\", nargs=\"?\")\n+    validate_parser.set_defaults(handler=_cmd_validate)\n+\n+    run_parser = subparsers.add_parser(\"run\", help=\"Run or dry-run one run_parser.add_argument(\"--input\", action=\"append\", default=[], metavar=\"NAME=VALUE\", help=\"Generic performer input; may be repeated.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--video-url\", \"--video\", dest=\"video_url\", help=\"Reachable http(s) video URL.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--title\", help=\"YouTube video title.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--description\", help=\"YouTube video description.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--tag\", action=\"append\", default=[], help=\"YouTube tag. May be repeated.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--tags\", action=\"append\", default=[], help=\"Comma-separated YouTube tags.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--privacy-status\", default=None, help=\"YouTube privacy status: private, unlisted, or public.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--playlist-id\", help=\"Optional YouTube playlist ID.\")\n+    run_parser.add_argument(\"--made-for-kids\", action=\"store_true\", help=\"Mark the video as made for kids.\")\n+    run_parser.set_defaults(handler=_cmd_run)\n+    return parser\n+\n+\n+def _cmd_list(args: argparse.Namespace, registry: PerformerRegistry) -> int:\n+    performers = registry.list()\n+    if args.json:\n+        print(registry.to_json())\n+        return 0\n+    for performer in performers:\n+        print(f\"{performer.id}\\t{performer.name}\")\n+    return 0\n+\n+\n+def _cmd_inspect(args: argparse.Namespace, registry: PerformerRegistry) -> int:\n+    performer = registry.get(args.performer_id)\n+    if args.json:\n+        print(performer.to_json())\n+        return 0\n+    print(f\"id: {performer.id}\")\n+    print(f\"name: {performer.name}\")\n+    print(f\"version: {performer.version}\")\n+    if performer.description:\n+        print(f\"description: {performer.description}\")\n+    if performer.inputs:\n+        print(\"inputs:\")\n+        for performer_input in performer.inputs:\n+            required = \"required\" if performer_input.required else \"optional\"\n+            print(f\"  - {performer_input.name} ({performer_input.type}, {required})\")\n+    return 0\n+\n+\n+def _cmd_validate(args: argparse.Namespace, registry: PerformerRegistry) -> int:\n+    registry.validate_all()\n+    performers = [registry.get(args.performer_id)] if args.performer_id else registry.list()\n+    if args.performer_id:\n+        print(f\"{args.performer_id}: ok\")\n+    else:\n+        print(f\"{len(performers)} performer(s): ok\")\n+    return 0\n+\n+\n+def _cmd_run(args: argparse.Namespace, registry: PerformerRegistry) -> int:\n+    inputs = _run_inputs(args)\n+    result = run_performer(\n+        PerformerRunRequest(\n+            performer_id=args.performer_id,\n+            inputs=inputs,\n+            dry_run=bool(args.dry_run),\n+        ),\n+        registry,\n+    )\n+ key = key.strip()\n+        if not key:\n+            raise ValueError(f\"invalid --input value {raw!r}; expected NAME=VALUE\")\n+        values[key] = value\n+    return values\n+\n+\n+if __name__ == > AGENT

Changed it across the public surface to `performers`.

What changed:
- Added `pipeline.py performers ...` as the primary CLI.
- Added `artagents/performers/` wrapper package.
- `upload.youtube` is now exposed as a performer.
- Conductors now use/display `child_performers`.
- `child_nodes` is still accepted as a legacy manifest field, but JSON/output now serializes `child_performers`.
- Docs and skill guidance now tell agents to use `performers`.
- Existing `nodes` CLI/module still works as the lower-level compatibility layer.

Verified:
- `100 passed, 2 xfailed, 4 subtests passed`
- Smoke-tested:
  - `pipeline.py performers list`
  - `pipeline.py conductors inspect builtin.hype`
  - `pipeline.py performers run builtin.render --dry-run`
  - `pipeline.py performers run upload.youtube --dry-run`

I did not physically rename the internal `artagents/nodes/` implementation directory yet. That would be a bigger breaking cleanup; right now it is intentionally the compatibility backend while `performers` is the user-facing API.

> AGENT

Yes, conductors and orchestrators were the same concept here. I removed the “orchestrator” wording from the user-facing ArtAgents docs/code comments and made that layer consistently `conductors`.

I would not make performers conductors too. The clean split is:

- `conductors`: coordinate a workflow and call other things.
- `performers`: do one executable action like render, transcribe, run Moirae, upload to YouTube.

So: all orchestrators are conductors, but not all performers should be conductors.

Also, the big cleanup test run passed before this wording patch: `130 passed, 2 xfailed, 4 subtests passed`.

> DEVELOPER

sorry, meant in was conductors and performeres

> AGENT

No, I’d keep `conductors` and `performers` separate.

They’re related, but not the same job:

- `conductors` decide sequencing, inputs, dependencies, and which actions to call.
- `performers` are the callable actions themselves: render, upload, run VibeComfy, run Moirae, transcribe, etc.

If we made everything a conductor, we’d lose useful meaning. A YouTube upload or render step doesn’t “conduct” anything; it performs one task. The orchestra metaphor works well as:

`conductor -> performers`

So I’d keep it exactly as that, and avoid `orchestrator` as a third term.

> DEVELOPER

yeah that's what i meant, everything is rolls into them

> AGENT

Yes, that’s the right model: every executable thing should be either a `conductor` or a `performer`. I’m just going to make that explicit in the docs/skill text so future agents don’t reintroduce `orchestrator`, `node`, or another middle term.

> AGENT

It’s much better now, but I’d call it **solid and maintainable**, not perfectly elegant.

What’s good:
- Clear model: `conductors` coordinate, `performers` execute.
- Real implementation moved under `artagents/performers/`.
- `artagents/nodes/` is now just a compatibility shim.
- Curated tools now live under `artagents/performers/curated/`.
- Tests and docs mostly use performer language.
- Focused suite passes: `130 passed, 2 xfailed, 4 subtests passed`.

Remaining inelegance:
- `artagents.nodes` and `pipeline.py nodes` still exist for backwards compatibility.
- Shared contract primitives are still internally named `NodePort` / `NodeOutput`, with `PerformerPort` / `PerformerOutput` aliases. That’s okay technically, but not pristine.
- A few tests still explicitly cover the legacy `nodes` shim, which is intentional but visually noisy.

So: yes, the architecture is now good. If we want it truly pristine, the next pass is a breaking cleanup: remove the `nodes` shim entirely and rename the shared contract primitives at the source.
